clinicalPearls: Stress urinary incontinence is the involuntary leakage of urine on effort, exertion, coughing or sneezing, reflecting failure of the sphincteric closure mechanism to withstand rises in abdominal pressure.
In women it is usually related to urethral hypermobility from pelvic floor and support weakness after childbirth and with ageing, or to intrinsic sphincter deficiency; the two frequently coexist.
In men it is most commonly iatrogenic, particularly following radical prostatectomy or other prostatic surgery that damages the sphincteric mechanism.
Mixed urinary incontinence, combining stress and urgency components, is common, and the more bothersome component should guide initial treatment.
A cough stress test demonstrating synchronous leakage, together with a bladder diary and pad testing, supports the diagnosis and quantifies severity.
Supervised pelvic floor muscle training is the first-line treatment and benefits both women and men, including after prostatectomy.

Surgical options in women include the midurethral sling and colposuspension, while intrinsic sphincter deficiency and post-prostatectomy incontinence may require slings or an artificial urinary sphincter.
Urodynamic assessment is reserved for complex, mixed, recurrent or pre-surgical cases and to confirm the diagnosis when it is unclear.
reference.pathophysiology: Continence during effort depends on the urethra remaining a competent, well-supported closure mechanism so that intraurethral pressure exceeds intravesical pressure when abdominal pressure suddenly rises. In stress urinary incontinence this mechanism fails by two overlapping routes. Loss of anatomical support, from weakening of the pelvic floor musculature, endopelvic fascia and vaginal wall attachments, allows the bladder neck and proximal urethra to descend and rotate (urethral hypermobility), so abdominal pressure is no longer transmitted equally to the urethra. Alternatively, or additionally, intrinsic sphincter deficiency, from denervation, scarring, atrophy or surgical damage, leaves the urethra unable to generate adequate closure pressure regardless of support. Contributing factors include vaginal childbirth, ageing and oestrogen deficiency, obesity, chronically raised intra-abdominal pressure, pelvic surgery and, in men, prostatic surgery. The result is leakage synchronous with transient increases in abdominal pressure and no accompanying detrusor contraction.
additionalDifferentials: Ectopic ureter presenting with continuous leakage
Functional incontinence from mobility or cognitive impairment
Extraurethral leakage or vaginal discharge mistaken for urine
additionalInvestigations: Cough stress test with a comfortably full bladder
Pad test to quantify leakage severity
Urinalysis and culture to exclude infection
Multichannel urodynamics in complex, mixed or recurrent cases
Cystourethroscopy or imaging when fistula, diverticulum or prior mesh complication is suspected
redFlags: Continuous leakage suggesting a fistula or ectopic ureter rather than true stress incontinence
Associated haematuria, pain or a pelvic mass
Significant post-void residual indicating retention with overflow
New neurological symptoms suggesting a neurogenic cause
Recurrent incontinence or pain after previous continence surgery or mesh insertion
reference.prognosis: Conservative pelvic floor muscle training improves or cures symptoms in a substantial proportion of patients, and appropriately selected surgery achieves high continence rates. Outcomes are less favourable with severe intrinsic sphincter deficiency, obesity, previous failed surgery and a large mixed urgency component.
pitfalls: Missing a coexisting overactive bladder component and operating on a patient whose main problem is urgency
Failing to exclude a fistula or ectopic ureter when leakage is actually continuous rather than effort related
Offering surgery before an adequate trial of supervised pelvic floor training
Overlooking chronic retention with overflow, which mimics stress leakage but requires very different management
Neglecting reversible contributors such as obesity, constipation, chronic cough and atrophic changes
references: European Association of Urology Guidelines on urinary incontinence
International Continence Society standardisation of terminology
